prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: There, The, Just

outputs.L1:
There is magic in decay—  
a dance to be done  
for the rotting, the maggot-strewn  
piles of flesh that heap  
upon the dung-ridden earth,  
and for the damp that gathers  
and rusts and defiles.

There is a bit of this  
in even the most zoetic soul—  
the dancing child’s arms,  
flailing to an old ska song,  
conduct the day-old flies  
away to whatever rank  
native is closest.

Just today,  
I was walking along the river  
with my daughter in my backpack,  
and I opened my email  
on my phone, and Duffie  
had sent me a poem  
called “Compost.” I read it  
to my little girl and started  
to explain, before I was three  
words in, when Selma started  
yelling, “Daddy, Daddy, snake!”

In the path was a snake,  
belly up and still nerve-twitching—  
the ghost of some passing  
bicycle or horse.

“Pretty,” Selma said.

“Yes,” I said. And underneath my yes,  
another yes: the yes to my body,  
just beginning to show signs  
of slack; and another, my grasping  
in the dark for affirming flesh  
that, in turn, says, “Yes, yes,  
let’s rot together—but not until  
we’ve drained what sap  
is left in these trees.”

And I wake in the morning  
and think of the coroner  
calling to ask what color  
my father’s eyes were,  
and I asked, “Why? Why can’t  
you just look?”—and the coroner,  
matter-of-factly, says, “Decay.”

Do you want some eggs, my love?  
I have a new way of preparing them.  
And look—look outside. I think this weather  
has the chance of holding.
outputs.L2:
Something wondrous lives in decomposition—  
a ritual movement meant for what spoils:  
for heaps of meat, crawling with larvae,  
stacked on manure-soaked ground,  
for the wetness that collects there,  
corroding, staining, ruining.

Some portion of that exists  
even in the most lively spirit—  
a child dancing, arms thrown about  
to an old ska tune,  
as if directing yesterday’s flies  
toward the nearest foul home  
they can claim.

Only today,  
I was walking beside the river  
with my daughter riding on my back.  
I checked my email on my phone,  
and Duffie had sent a poem  
titled “Compost.”  
I began reading it aloud  
to my little girl,  
and I had barely started  
to explain it  
when Selma cried out,  
Daddy, Daddy, snake!

There, on the trail,  
lay a snake,  
turned on its back,  
motionless except for the last small spasms  
of nerves—  
the remnant, perhaps,  
of a bicycle or horse passing over it.

Pretty, Selma said.  
Yes, I answered.  
And beneath that yes  
was another yes:  
one spoken to my own body,  
which has only begun  
to loosen and sag.  
And beneath that, another—  
my reaching through darkness  
for living skin that answers back,  
yes, yes,  
let us decay side by side,  
but only after  
we have taken every last drop  
of sap these trees still hold.

And in the morning I wake  
thinking of the coroner  
calling to ask  
the color of my father’s eyes.  
I asked, Why?  
Why can’t you simply look?  
And the coroner replied plainly:  
Decay.

Would you like eggs, my love?  
I’ve found a different way  
to cook them.  
And see—look out there—  
I think this weather  
may last.
outputs.L3:
The poem presents decay as both a natural process and a strangely magical force that exists within all living things. Rather than treating decomposition only as something horrifying or repulsive, the speaker recognizes it as part of the hidden energy of life itself. Every body carries within it the possibility of breakdown, transformation, and return to the earth. In this way, decay becomes inseparable from vitality: to be alive is also to be moving, however slowly, toward decline.

This meditation begins during a walk with the speaker’s daughter, when they come across a dead snake. The encounter is ordinary and startling at once. The snake’s body, marked by death and decomposition, prompts the speaker to think about beauty, mortality, and the physical vulnerability shared by all creatures. The snake may be ruined or decaying, yet it still possesses a certain fascination. Its body becomes an image through which the speaker considers how death alters beauty without entirely erasing it.

The sight of the snake also leads the speaker inward, toward an awareness of their own aging body. The snake’s decomposition mirrors the speaker’s sense of bodily decline, reminding them that human flesh is subject to the same natural processes. This recognition creates an urgency around intimacy and love. The speaker becomes conscious of wanting closeness, touch, and tenderness before death makes such experiences impossible. Bodily decay is therefore not only a symbol of fear, but also a reminder of desire and the need to connect while there is still time.

The poem’s reflection on mortality deepens through the memory of the coroner describing the speaker’s father’s body after death. This recollection makes decay personal and familial rather than merely abstract. The father’s decomposed body forces the speaker to confront the material reality of death: the body does not remain whole, dignified, or untouched, but changes according to physical processes beyond human control. The coroner’s clinical discussion intensifies the poem’s emotional weight, showing how death reduces even a beloved person to a body undergoing decomposition.

Yet the poem does not remain solely in darkness. It contrasts death and bodily breakdown with ordinary gestures of love and continuity: sharing food, caring for a child, desiring intimacy, and hoping for good weather. These small human acts do not cancel mortality, but they stand beside it as forms of resistance and consolation. The poem suggests that life is meaningful not because it escapes decay, but because love, appetite, tenderness, and hope persist in the face of it. Death is always present, but so are the daily rituals that make existence bearable and beautiful.
outputs.L4:
The poem is a meditation on decay, mortality, and the stubborn persistence of life. It approaches these large themes not through abstract argument, but through close observation and personal memory. The speaker notices rotting matter, the body of a dead snake, the presence of a child, the memory of a father, and the quiet intimacy of domestic life. These details create a movement between the natural world and the human world, showing that death is not separate from ordinary experience but woven into it.

The images of decay are physical and direct. Rotting matter and the dead snake remind the reader that all living things are vulnerable to breakdown and disappearance. Yet the poem does not treat decay simply as horror or loss. Instead, it presents decomposition as part of a larger cycle in which life continues. What dies becomes part of the ground, part of the world that nourishes future growth. In this way, the poem suggests that mortality is not only an ending, but also a condition of renewal.

The speaker’s observations are deeply personal. The encounter with death in nature leads to thoughts of family, especially the memory of a father. This connection gives the poem emotional weight. The father’s absence becomes part of the same pattern the speaker sees in the natural world: people pass away, bodies fail, and yet their presence remains in memory, habit, and love. The poem therefore treats grief not as something separate from daily life, but as something carried within it.

At the same time, the poem is filled with signs of tenderness and vitality. A walk with a child becomes more meaningful because it takes place in a world where everything is temporary. Domestic moments, such as sharing breakfast, gain depth because they are fragile and passing. The poem recognizes that love exists alongside decay, not apart from it. The knowledge of death does not diminish affection; instead, it intensifies it.

By bringing together rotting matter, a dead animal, family memory, and ordinary intimacy, the poem shows that life and death are inseparable. Its vision is not despairing, but accepting. It finds beauty in the fact that even the most ordinary moments are touched by mortality. Walking with a child, remembering a father, or sharing a meal becomes profound because these acts are brief, embodied, and vulnerable. The poem ultimately suggests that to accept decay is also to accept the fullness of life: its tenderness, its losses, and its enduring capacity for love.
outputs.L5:
There is a quiet power in the smallest words. The words we use every day often pass unnoticed, yet they shape how we think, speak, and connect with others. “There” can point us toward a place, a memory, or a possibility. “The” gives something importance, making it specific and real. “Just” can mean fairness, simplicity, or a moment that has only recently happened.

Together, these words remind us that language does not always need to be complicated to be meaningful. There is beauty in the simple phrase, the clear idea, and the just decision. Sometimes, the smallest words carry the greatest weight.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a contemporary free-verse poem about finding beauty and affirmation in decay, including a walk by a river with a young daughter, a dead snake, compost, aging, desire, and a memory of a coroner asking about the speaker’s father’s eye color.
counterfactuals.output:
**Inheritance with River**

My daughter walks ahead of me  
in the extravagant way of children,  
as if the path has been unrolled  
for the purpose of her feet.

The river keeps talking to itself,  
brown and silver, shouldering light  
past beer cans, willow roots,  
the soft collapse of last year’s leaves.

She stops.

A snake lies on the trail,  
dead long enough to be harmless,  
recent enough to still be snake—  
black ribbon, split mouth,  
a little astonishment  
left in the shape of it.

Beautiful, she says,  
then looks at me to see  
if she is allowed.

Yes, I tell her.  
Beautiful.

What else can I call  
the body’s brief architecture  
once the tenant is gone?  
What else can I say  
to the flies stippling its shine,  
to the ants entering  
like careful relatives?

At home, the compost steams  
in its green-black patience:  
coffee grounds, pear cores,  
the bruised lettuce, eggshell moon-shards,  
everything we could not keep  
becoming what will feed us.

I am trying to learn from this.

My face has begun  
its slow conversation with gravity.  
My hands are my mother’s hands now,  
veins lifted like river maps.  
Desire still rises in me,  
unreasonable and bright—  
not despite the body’s weather  
but through it,

the way mushrooms shoulder up  
from rot,  
the way a fig splits open  
when it is sweetest.

Once, after my father died,  
a coroner called and asked  
his eye color.

I was standing in a grocery store  
between the apples and the onions,  
holding the phone to my ear  
as if it were a shell  
that had remembered the sea.

Blue, I said.  
No—gray.  
No—  
I don’t know.

How could I not know?

All my life I had been looked at  
by those eyes.  
Corrected, adored,  
measured, missed.  
And still, when the state needed  
a box filled in,  
I could not summon the shade  
of my father’s seeing.

My daughter crouches now  
beside the snake  
without touching it.

Its scales catch the afternoon  
in little panes of oil.  
The river goes on spending itself.  
A heron lifts from the shallows  
like a thought  
deciding to leave the body.

Soon the snake will loosen  
into the mouths of beetles.  
Soon the leaves will darken  
under rain.  
Soon my daughter will be taller  
than my shoulder,  
then gone down paths  
I cannot follow.

This is not a tragedy yet.

This is the world saying  
yes with all its mouths—  
yes to the broken stalk,  
yes to the fruit gone soft,  
yes to the heat in the heap,  
yes to the wanting  
that outlives the smooth skin,  
yes to the father  
becoming question,  
yes to the daughter  
bending close to death  
and finding shimmer.

We stand there  
by the river,  
two animals breathing  
beside another animal  
no longer breathing,

and everything  
is being taken apart  
so tenderly  
I almost believe

nothing is lost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a lyrical, unsettling poem in the style of modern confessional nature poetry, beginning with the idea that “there is magic in decay” and moving from rot and maggots to parenthood, mortality, love, breakfast, and hopeful weather.
counterfactuals.output:
There is magic in decay—  
not the pretty kind, not the moon  
silvering the orchard into forgiveness,  
but the wet black seam  
where the pear gives in,  
where flies kneel and shimmer  
like little priests of appetite.

I have watched maggots work  
their pale commas through the fallen fruit,  
writing the first draft  
of everything returning.  
I wanted to be disgusted.  
Instead I thought of my child  
asleep in the next room,  
mouth open to the dark,  
dreaming perhaps of milk,  
or nothing, which is mercy.

How strange, to love a body  
you cannot keep.  
To button the coat,  
to cut the grapes in half,  
to check the fevered forehead  
as if your palm were law.  
All morning I perform  
these small denials of death:  
toast, butter, blueberries rinsed  
in a cracked blue bowl,  
the kettle lifting its thin cry  
to the ceiling.

Outside, the compost steams.  
A sparrow worries the hedge.  
The world is making and unmaking  
itself without asking me  
to be brave.  
Still, I stand at the sink  
with my hands in warm water,  
feeling the dishes slide clean  
as bones in rain.

My child calls for more jam.  
The sun, uncertain but present,  
pushes through the cloud bank  
like a thumb through bruised fruit.  
Some weather is coming—  
soft, maybe, green at the edges.  
The kind that enters quietly,  
then fills every broken thing  
with light.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a free verse poem with no stanza breaks about decomposition as a kind of dance, featuring ska music, flies, a child named Selma in a backpack, an email from Duffie containing a poem called “Compost,” and the line “Let’s rot together.”
counterfactuals.output:
The horn section starts up in the heat,  
ska bright as tin cans kicked down an alley,  
and the dead leaves find their rhythm,  
heel-toe, heel-toe,  
fungus lifting its soft white gloves  
from under the mulch.  
Flies arrive like black notes  
on the sweating page of the afternoon,  
their wings all brass and jitter,  
their feet tasting every sweetness  
the world is brave enough to surrender.  
Selma is in a backpack,  
small knees tucked like secrets,  
watching the garden breathe and loosen,  
watching apple cores collapse  
into a darker kind of music.  
Someone’s phone pings—  
an email from Duffie,  
subject line: Compost,  
and inside it a poem called “Compost”  
where every ending turns its face  
toward the soil and grins.  
The worms begin their skank,  
side to side through rind and root,  
the beetles click time,  
the mold blooms green applause,  
and even the bones of last season’s flowers  
seem to lean into the offbeat.  
“Let’s rot together.”  
The sentence hangs warm in the air,  
not a curse, not a dare,  
but an invitation  
to join the grand unfastening,  
to become crumb, rain-dark,  
root-ready, beloved by flies,  
to give up the stiff choreography  
of staying whole  
and enter the dance floor  
beneath everything living.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an original poem that blends the grotesque and the tender: rotting flesh, dung, dampness, a dead snake on a path, a father’s decaying body, a lover making eggs, and the possibility that the weather will hold.
counterfactuals.output:
**Weather Holding**

In the ditch, the rain keeps its little mouth open,  
drinking from the blackened leaves,  
from the slick rope of a dead snake  
curled like a question someone stepped over  
and did not answer.

The path smells of dung and mushrooms,  
of damp wool, of meat giving up  
its argument with the world.  
Even the flies seem holy at their work,  
small priests in green vestments  
blessing the rotting flesh  
with their many hands.

My father is becoming earth in the next town over.  
His body, once a door I knocked on,  
once a weather report, a wallet, a cough,  
is loosening beneath the varnished lid—  
cheek caving, blood gone dark,  
the bright machinery of him  
quietly rusting in its room.

I think of him while you stand at the stove,  
barefoot, cracking eggs into a bowl.  
The shells break with such clean, shy sounds.  
Your wrist turns, and the yolks bloom—  
two small suns trembling in their milk.  
You salt them, hum a song I almost know,  
and the kitchen window fogs with our breathing.

Outside, the yard is mud and nettle.  
A dog has nosed something foul from the hedge.  
The drains are full. The sky lowers itself  
like a hand on a fevered head.

Still, you butter the pan.  
Still, there is bread on the table,  
a blue cup, a knife, your shoulder  
warm where I touch it.

The dead keep changing shape without us.  
The snake thins into the path.  
The dung steams softly in the field.  
My father enters the roots by degrees,  
not vanished, only traveling  
through the dark mouths of things.

And you, turning the eggs over gently,  
as if waking a child, say  
the clouds may pass north of here,  
the wind has shifted,  
there’s every chance

the weather will hold.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a first-person narrative poem exploring death, bodily decay, and domestic love, where the speaker reads a compost poem to his daughter during a walk and later recalls being unable to identify his dead father’s eyes because of decay.
counterfactuals.output:
**Compost**

I pushed my daughter in the stroller  
past the community gardens,  
where the rain had worked all night  
at softening the earth  
and every plot smelled opened—  
black tea, wet leaves, worms  
turning their blind mouths through rot.

She had asked for a poem.  
Not the moon one, not the one  
with the bear going over the mountain,  
but the compost poem,  
the one I had made up badly  
on another walk, when she was two  
and loved any word  
that sounded like a thing being stirred.

So I read it from my phone  
in the voice she liked:

*Apple core, coffee ground,*  
*eggshell, rind,*  
*everything lost*  
*comes back kind.*  

She laughed at *rind*.  
A sparrow jumped the fence  
and vanished under the kale.  
I said, See, even the dead leaves  
are feeding something.

She asked if people do that.

And because I am her father,  
which means I am always standing  
between the world and its answers  
with my bare hands raised,  
I said, Yes.  
Eventually.  
Gently as I could,  
as if the word itself were a blanket.

At home that evening  
I washed the dirt from her socks,  
set rice to steam,  
cut carrots into small bright coins.  
My wife stood at the sink  
with her sleeves pushed up,  
soap shining on her wrists,  
and I loved her so suddenly  
it frightened me—  
the ordinary mercy of dishes,  
the lamp over the table,  
our daughter singing nonsense  
to a spoon.

How can a body know  
it is temporary  
and still reach  
for another body in the dark?  
How can the hand,  
made of meat and future ash,  
learn the shape of a cheek  
and call that knowledge home?

Later, after the story,  
after the bathwater cooled  
and the plastic ducks lay stranded  
on the tub’s white shore,  
I remembered my father.

Not as he was  
holding a hammer,  
or asleep in his chair  
with the news falling blue  
across his face,  
but on the metal table  
at the funeral home,  
when they asked if I could identify him.

His mouth was almost his mouth.  
His jaw had kept  
some stubborn argument  
with the living.  
But the eyes—

I had known those eyes  
as weather, as warning,  
as porchlight, as a door  
I could not open.  
I had watched them close  
in anger, soften over soup,  
fill once when my daughter  
placed a sticker on his hand.

And yet decay had taken them  
past resemblance.  
The skin around them darkened,  
the lids swollen,  
the sockets altered  
by that first private work  
the body begins  
when no one is watching.

I stood there  
like a child at a test  
for which there was no study.  
I wanted to say,  
No, bring me my father’s eyes.  
Bring back the exact brown  
that held my face  
and failed me  
and loved me  
in its own buried language.

But death had already  
started translating him  
into earth.

So I nodded.  
I signed.  
I let the sheet return  
like snow over a field  
before spring takes it.

Tonight my daughter sleeps  
with one arm flung upward,  
as if answering a question  
asked by a star.  
In the kitchen, the compost pail  
waits under the sink:  
banana peel, carrot tops,  
the softening heel of bread  
no one wanted.

Tomorrow I will carry it out.  
I will tip the small bucket  
into the larger dark.  
Steam will rise  
if the pile is warm enough,  
a breath from all that breaking.

And I will think:  
this is what love does, too—  
not save us from vanishing,  
not keep the eyes clear,  
not seal the body  
against its own undoing,  
but hold us while we change.

My daughter will run ahead  
on the path,  
her boots bright with mud.  
She will ask for the poem again.  
I will give it to her,  
my little spell against nothing,  
my little truth with a handle:

*Apple core, coffee ground,*  
*eggshell, rind,*  
*everything lost*  
*comes back kind.*
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
